meta.title: Metering and meter reads
meta.subtitle: The market settles every half hour. Most meters are read a few times a year. Everything else follows from that gap.
meta.one_line: GB electricity is settled in half-hourly periods, but for most of the last decade most domestic meters could not report at that grain — so the industry settled them against a national average shape scaled to an estimate of their annual consumption, and corrected the difference months or years later. A supplier bills what it believes, buys against what it forecasts, and finds out what was true afterwards.
meta.wall_placement: Public-reality commons only. Settlement periods, profile classes, the read cadence and the back-billing rule are published features of the GB market — readable by anyone, so readable by the simulated company too, the same way a real supplier reads the BSC and its licence conditions. Nothing on this page is a simulation internal.

claim_freshness.source: Elexon BSC settlement arrangements and load-profile guidance; Ofgem standard licence conditions on billing and back-billing; the MHHS programme's published milestones.
claim_freshness.route: Written from the published arrangements and cross-checked against this repository's own implementations and their recorded provenance (docs/data-sources/profile-class-1.md, simulation/meter_reads.py).

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: Great Britain settles electricity in half-hourly periods — 48 a day, every day — but for most of the past decade most domestic meters could not report at anything like that resolution, so the industry settled them against a **national average shape** scaled to an **estimate** of their annual consumption, and reconciled the difference months later. Almost every operational problem a domestic supplier has, from a shocking catch-up bill to a hedge that was bought against the wrong volume, is a consequence of that one gap.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
The market wants to know how much electricity you used between 17:00 and 17:30 last Tuesday. Your meter, if it is an older one, can tell you roughly how much you have used since someone last looked at it — which might have been in March.

So the industry does something reasonable and slightly unnerving: it **assumes**. It takes a published curve describing how a typical household of your type uses electricity across a day and a season, scales it so the year adds up to what it thinks your annual consumption is, and settles you against that. Your actual pattern is not used, because nobody knows it.

Two things follow. The first is that your **bill** and your **settlement** are different objects: the bill is what your supplier charges you, the settlement is what your supplier is charged for you. They are reconciled later, and "later" can mean years.

The second is the estimated bill. If no read has arrived, your supplier still has to bill you, so it estimates. When a real reading finally turns up, the difference lands as a correction. If the estimates were low for long enough, that correction is a large unexpected bill — which is why there is a rule about it: a supplier generally cannot bill you for energy used more than **twelve months** ago where the failure to bill was its own. Anything older than that is written off, and the write-off is a real cost that falls on the supplier.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
**The settlement period is the unit.** Half an hour, 48 per day, numbered 1–48 from midnight. Every wholesale purchase, every imbalance charge and every network charge lands in one. This is not an implementation convention; it is the resolution the market clears at.

**Two settlement classes.** A meter that reports half-hourly is settled **HH** — on what it actually did. A meter that does not is settled **NHH** (non-half-hourly), against a **profile class**: a published average shape for a category of customer. Profile Class 1 is domestic unrestricted, Class 2 is domestic with a restricted (Economy 7) meter, and the commercial classes run on up. The shape says *when*; a separate figure says *how much*.

**That figure is an estimate, and it has a name.** For electricity it is the **EAC** — Estimated Annual Consumption — recalculated as reads arrive. For gas it is the **AQ**, Annual Quantity. Both are the supplier's working belief about a customer's yearly volume, and both are what forward purchases are sized against. An EAC that is wrong is a hedge that is wrong.

**Settlement is not one event.** An initial run happens on incomplete information, and reconciliation runs follow at increasing distances — the industry's own recognition that the truth arrives late. A supplier's position in a period can be revised long after it thought the period was closed.

**Reads arrive irregularly, and their quality is recorded.** A reading is *actual* (someone or something measured it) or *estimated* (the supplier inferred it). Bills carry that distinction on their face, and a run of estimated bills is resolved by the next actual read — which is where a catch-up correction comes from.

**Smart metering, and then MHHS.** A smart meter can report half-hourly, which collapses the gap at source. But installing the meters is not the same as settling on them: **Market-wide Half-Hourly Settlement** is the programme to move the whole market onto actual half-hourly data rather than profiles. Its dates have moved more than once, and any supplier's readiness is a programme position rather than a switch that flips.

**Gas is a different animal.** It balances daily rather than half-hourly, meters are read on cadences that vary by size class, and the residual between what was measured and what the network says flowed is a real reconciliation quantity — **unidentified gas** — that gets shared out among shippers. Gas has the same estimate-then-correct structure with different machinery.

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
**A half-hourly meter's day has a shape, and the shape is the household.** Electric heating shows as a winter day several times the size of a summer one; a heat pump or storage heating shows as a block at particular hours; an EV shows as a deep overnight trough that is not a trough. A profile-class account has none of this — its "shape" is a national average, so every account in the class looks alike by construction.

**Estimated reads cluster, they do not scatter.** They come in runs, because the thing that produces them — nobody reading the meter — persists. A dataset where estimated and actual alternate randomly is not modelling the mechanism.

**Catch-up corrections are lumpy and signed.** A run of under-estimates resolves as one large charge; over-estimates resolve as a credit. The distribution should be skewed, not symmetric, and it should have a hard edge where the twelve-month rule bites.

**EAC should converge and then wander.** It moves toward the truth as reads arrive, then drifts as the household changes — a new occupant, an EV, a heat pump. An EAC that is stable to four figures for a decade is a table, not an estimate.

live_evidence.heading: What this simulation actually does
live_evidence.body:
**Both classes exist, and they are settled differently.** Accounts with half-hourly metering are settled against real half-hourly series (`sim/hh_data/`); profile-class accounts are settled against the published **Group Average Demand** shape for Profile Class 1, taken from the UKERC Energy Data Centre archive rather than invented — the full provenance trail, including which source was used and why the modern API could not supply it, is recorded in `docs/data-sources/profile-class-1.md`. Every settlement period is priced on its own: the engine walks all 48 and, on a time-of-use tariff, applies the peak or off-peak rate for *that* half hour.

**Reads are actual or estimated, and the bill says which.** The billing path decides per bill whether a real read arrived, bills the estimate at the real unit rate when it did not, and folds the reconciled correction onto the next actual bill — capped where the back-billing rule applies, with the written-off portion treated as a cost rather than quietly dropped. A closing account is forced to resolve on a final read rather than leaving a run of estimates permanently unreconciled.

**You can see the two classes side by side.** [Explore](../../explore/#used) draws a real half-hourly day for the accounts that have one — a named date, 48 metered half-hours — and for the rest it draws nothing and says why: their meter is read a handful of times a year, so neither the supplier nor the page can know when the electricity was used. That absence is the honest rendering of this page's subject.

**MHHS is tracked as a programme, not assumed.** The company carries a readiness position against the programme's milestones rather than a boolean.

residuals.heading: What this page does not settle
residuals.body:
**The read-cadence rule is not fully verified in our own implementation, and it is marked as such in the code.** `simulation/meter_reads.py` carries an explicit warning that the precise licence-condition cadence it models is unconfirmed; the twelve-month back-billing principle beside it is confirmed. That is the honest state: one rule checked, one modelled on secondary guidance and labelled.

**The profile shape is a real published series from a 1997 reference year.** It is genuine Group Average Demand data, not a fabrication — and it is also nearly three decades old. GB domestic load has changed since (lighting, appliances, electrification of heat and transport). Using it is defensible for the shape's *structure* and questionable for its *level*, and this page does not pretend the question is closed.

**Reconciliation is described here and not fully modelled.** The simulation settles and it corrects bills, but it does not reproduce the industry's multi-run reconciliation timetable as a first-class object with positions revised at each run.

**Unidentified gas is named, not implemented.** The gas-side residual is a real quantity with real money attached; this simulation does not produce one.

scope_delta.heading: Where the simulation stops
scope_delta.body: No DCC: there is no smart-metering communications layer, no SMETS1/SMETS2 distinction, and no device estate to fail. No consent model — a real supplier must ask before it may use half-hourly data for anything beyond settlement, and that permission is itself a customer relationship. No change-of-supplier read disputes, no meter faults, no tampering, no access refusals; every read that arrives here is either genuine or an honest estimate, where a real supplier also has readings that are wrong. No MHHS migration: the programme is tracked, not enacted, so no account changes settlement class mid-run. And no industry data flows — the messages real suppliers actually exchange are absent, which is precisely the seam that would be swapped for real endpoints at go-live.
